You talk about what "people" say and do: impersonal si (si dice, si vive bene), ci si (ci si abitua), si in compound tenses (si è detto, si è arrivati stanchi), uno, la gente, è risaputo che, si mormora che.
you get used to it, we get used to it
They say Valeria wants to stand as a candidate.
In the Oltrarno people live well, but they pay a lot.
You get used to anything, even the noise.
There was a lot of talk about the trattoria.
When you are tired, you say the wrong things.
To use impersonal si in the third person singular: si dice, si vive, si mangia bene.
To use ci si with reflexive verbs: ci si abitua, ci si alza presto.
To make the adjective plural after impersonal si: quando si è stanchi.
To use impersonal si in compound tenses: si è parlato, si è arrivati.
To generalise with uno, la gente, tutti, è risaputo che.
To report rumours: si dice / si mormora / pare che + subjunctive.

Florence, January. Valeria Conti has decided to stand for the neighbourhood council in the spring elections. She is collecting signatures at the Santo Spirito market, with Graziella beside her. The fruit seller is sceptical.
So what people say is true? You're standing as a candidate?
It's true. And we're collecting signatures. We need two hundred by February.
Well. People whisper that you worked for that lot from Milan. The ones who wanted to close the trattoria.
That's true too. And that's exactly why I know how to stop them.
Listen, dear. When you're young, you make mistakes. What matters is what you do afterwards.
Maybe. But in politics, as everyone knows, people promise a lot and do little.
You're right. Then let's do it this way: I promise you nothing. I'm just asking you what should be done, in your opinion.
In my opinion? You should be able to park the van in the morning without getting a fine.
I'll note it down. You see? That's how you start. One thing at a time.
And besides, it's well known: whoever eats my ribollita can't be a bad person.
All right, all right. Where do I sign?
"dove si firma?" = where do I sign?
Si + the verb in the third person singular = an action done "by anyone", "in general":
In the Oltrarno people live well.
The difference from passive si (chapter 57): there the verb has an object it agrees with (si vendono giornali); here it has no object (si vive bene).
When the verb is already reflexive (abituarsi, alzarsi), you can't say "si si". You say "ci si":
In campagna ci si alza presto.
Alle feste di Graziella ci si diverte.
NOT: "si si abitua". Correct: "ci si abitua".
The verb is singular, but the adjective or participle referring to "people in general" is PLURAL:
Quando si è stanchi, si sbaglia.
When you're tired, you make mistakes.
Quando si è giovani, si fanno sbagli.
When you're young, you make mistakes.
It seems strange (singular verb, plural adjective), but it is logical: "si" means "people".
In compound tenses, impersonal si always uses essere:
Si è parlato molto della trattoria.
Practical rule: verbs that normally take avere have the participle in -o (si è parlato); those that take essere have the participle in the plural (si è partiti).
5. Other forms of generalisation and rumours
Uno non sa mai che cosa dire.
One never knows what to say.
È risaputo che la ribollita è buona.
si mormora / si dice che + subjunctive
Si mormora che sia una venduta.
People whisper that she has sold out.
"La gente" is singular in Italian: "la gente dice" (not "dicono"), although in Romanian you say "oamenii zic".
People got to the party late.
People whisper that she worked for Milan.
Per che cosa si candida Valeria?
Che cosa si mormora su Valeria?
Che ha lavorato per quelli di Milano
Che cosa dice Graziella sugli sbagli?
L’importante è quello che si fa dopo
Di poter parcheggiare il furgone senza multa
Che cosa fa alla fine la fruttivendola?
People say she wants to stand as a candidate.

In the Oltrarno, as everyone knows, news runs faster than the tram. Valeria Conti had told only three people, one January evening, at the trattoria: Graziella, Bellini and Mancini, who had promised not to write a single line "until it's official". The next morning, at the Santo Spirito market, the fruit seller already knew. By lunchtime the barman knew. In the evening, the baker had put a handwritten sign in his window: "People say Mrs Conti is standing as a candidate. We know nothing." Valeria saw it as she walked past and burst out laughing. "There you go," she said to Graziella. "The election campaign has started. And I wasn't the one who started it."

The idea had been born in December, after Pietro and Davide's debate tournament. Councillor Neri, at the end of the prize-giving, had taken Valeria aside. The neighbourhood council elections were in May, she had explained, and in the Oltrarno nobody ever stood, because, people said, "nothing changes anyway". "You know the property companies' figures better than they do," Neri had told her. "And you know the neighbourhood. Think about it." Valeria had thought about it for three weeks. Then, one evening, she had seen Pietro's crooked cup on the kitchen shelf, next to the plaque and Aldo's letters, and had decided.

To stand, two hundred signatures from residents had to be collected by the end of February. It seemed easy. It wasn't. In the neighbourhood, it was immediately discovered, not everyone remembered Valeria as the consultant who had saved the trattoria. Many remembered her as the manager from Arno Living, the one in the blue suit who at the April assembly had defended short-term rentals. And rumours, in the Oltrarno, are not easily forgotten. People whispered that she was still paid by Milan. People said she wanted a career in politics. Someone even claimed she had bought a house in the Parioli district, in Rome, although nobody really knew why Parioli of all places.

In the first week Valeria collected eleven signatures. Seven were from family. One was Bellini's, who signed with Ernesto's tiny brush "because important things are signed with the right tools". One was Lupino's, whom Pietro had helped to leave his paw print on a separate sheet, "as a symbol", although the electoral office would never have accepted it. Valeria began to lose heart. "You think you've done good," she said one evening, "and then you discover that people only remember the bad." Graziella poured her another glass of wine. "My dear," she said, "people don't remember. People talk. Which is something else."

Pietro was, once again, the one who had the right idea. "At the tournament," he said, "I won by agreeing with my opponent. Why don't you do the same? Instead of denying what people say, say it yourself first." Valeria looked at him without understanding. "Write a leaflet," Pietro explained, "with all the rumours going around. And under each rumour, the truth." Mancini, who was listening from the next table, looked up from his newspaper. "It's brilliant," he said. "It's called 'taking the bull by the horns'. In journalism, that's how it's done: when you can't stop a piece of gossip, you publish it first."

The leaflet came out a week later, printed by the print shop in San Frediano, the same one where Aldo had worked in 1974. It was yellow, written in big letters, and it was titled "People say that…". Below, in two columns, were the rumours and the answers. "People say Valeria Conti worked for Arno Living. — True. Six years. And she resigned when she understood what it was doing to the neighbourhood." "People say she is still paid by Milan. — False. She is paid by the council as a consultant, and her salary is public: 1,800 euros a month." "People say she bought a house in Parioli. — False. She rents in via dei Serragli, on the third floor, no lift."

At the print shop, the old owner, a gentleman of eighty-one with fingers still black with ink, read the leaflet before printing it. Then he looked up at Pietro, who had come to collect the copies. "You're Aldo's grandson," he said. It wasn't a question. Pietro nodded, surprised. "He worked here," the printer went on. "In '74. He set the pages by hand, letter by letter, and never got a subjunctive wrong. People said, in the print shop, that he was in love with the girl from the trattoria in via Maggio. He never admitted it." He smiled. "But every day, at lunchtime, he disappeared for an hour. And he came back with the face of someone who has eaten the best ribollita in Florence." For the five hundred copies of the leaflet, that day, he charged nothing.

The last rumour on the leaflet was the funniest, and had been added by Graziella at the last moment, without asking anyone's permission. "People say she can't cook. — True. But she eats ribollita in via Maggio three times a week, which, as is well known, is the closest thing to knowing how to cook." Valeria, when she read it, wanted to remove it. Pietro and Mancini persuaded her to leave it. "In politics," said Mancini, "you win with ideas. But you get votes with a laugh."

The leaflet went round the neighbourhood in three days. It was everywhere: on the bar counter, in the baker's window, on the trattoria tables, taped to the door of the haberdashery that had reopened in November. And something happened that nobody expected. People started stopping Valeria in the street, not to accuse her, but to talk. They stopped to tell her about their problems: the rising rent, the broken pavement, the van that couldn't be parked, the school without a gym. Valeria listened and noted everything in a notebook. She promised nothing. She only said: "I'll note it down. That's how you start."

Not everyone, of course, was happy. In those weeks another resident stood as well, the lawyer Bardi, an elegant gentleman who lived in a palazzo on the bank of the Arno and who, people said, had important friends at the city council. Bardi never spoke directly about Valeria. He preferred the impersonal form. "We all know how these things go," he told journalists. "One starts by saving a trattoria and ends up wanting to run the neighbourhood. One ought to be more careful, coming from certain companies." Mancini reproduced his sentences word for word in the "Gazzetta", with a one-line comment: "When people speak in the impersonal, it is usually because they don't want to sign what they say."

The following Saturday, at the Santo Spirito market, Valeria and Graziella set up a folding table between the fruit stall and the cheese stall. On the table were the yellow leaflets, the signature forms and a thermos labelled "herbal tea", which, of course, contained ribollita, offered to anyone who signed. Mancini said it was vote-buying. Graziella replied that, if feeding people was a crime, then she was a seventy-year-old criminal. The fruit seller, who three weeks earlier had spread half of the rumours, was the first to sign, after a long discussion about parking vans.

Then the baker signed. Then the barman. Then Rita, Davide's mother, who arrived from her night shift with dark circles under her eyes and signed without even reading, saying she trusted anyone who could count better than that lot from Milan. Then Efisio and Lucia, Davide's grandparents, who signed together, with the same pen, as they had done at their wedding in 1968. Then Lorenzo, who signed and offered to hand out leaflets in every bar in the neighbourhood. Then Rocco, the site foreman, who didn't live in the Oltrarno and so couldn't sign, but who wanted a leaflet anyway "to show my wife".

By lunchtime there were sixty-two signatures. By five, one hundred and four. The ribollita had run out at three, and Graziella had to send Pietro home to fetch a second pot. But the best moment of the day came at about six, as the market was closing. An elderly gentleman nobody knew came up to the table with the yellow leaflet in his hand. He had folded and unfolded it so many times that it looked like a letter. "I know you," he said to Valeria. "You were the one at the assembly. The one who ate ribollita alone, at the end, while everyone glared at her."

Valeria stiffened. She expected an accusation. Instead the gentleman smiled. "I was there," he said. "At the back of the hall. And I thought: this woman has courage. It takes courage to sit down and eat alone when everyone looks at you as an enemy. You understand a lot about a person from the way they eat when they're alone." He took the pen, signed and handed back the form. "My name is Guido," he said. "I was a shoemaker in via Toscanella, until two years ago. Then they tripled my rent and I closed. If you get onto the council, remember people like me." Valeria wrote his name in the notebook, underlined twice.

Graziella, who was filling her umpteenth cup of "herbal tea", turned round at the sound of the name. "Guido?" she said. "Guido of the shoes?" The gentleman looked at her more closely, then his face lit up. "Graziella! Ribollita!" They hugged across the table, knocking over half the leaflets. Guido had resoled her shoes for thirty years, Graziella told Valeria, the same black shoes she wore in the trattoria every day. "People in the neighbourhood said Graziella's shoes were eternal," laughed Guido. "They weren't eternal. I repaired them every six months." When she learned that Guido no longer worked, Graziella became serious. "Then who repairs my shoes now?" she asked. Nobody knew what to answer. Valeria added a line in her notebook: "Graziella's shoes."

That evening, at the trattoria, the signatures were counted: one hundred and thirty-one. Sixty-nine were still missing and ten days remained. There was a long discussion about how to find them. Bellini suggested going door to door, as people used to. Mancini suggested an article in the "Gazzetta". Lorenzo suggested a web page. Davide was the one who, in the end, suggested the simplest thing. "The school," he said. "The parents of the children in San Frediano. Nearly all of them are residents and nearly all of them have read the leaflet. You just have to ask them at the school gate, in the afternoon." Rita, his mother, looked at him with pride. "You can tell you grew up among restorers," she said. "You always find the smallest solution."

Before they started, Valeria gave the two boys just one rule. "You never ask for a signature," she said. "You ask for a problem. The signature comes afterwards, by itself." So Pietro and Davide learned to stop parents at the school gate with a different question: "Excuse me, in your opinion what should be changed in the neighbourhood?" The answers were long, sometimes angry, sometimes funny. One mother complained that in the Oltrarno you can no longer find a place to buy a button. One father said people pay too much for parking and too little for work. One grandfather said that, in his day, everyone knew each other by name. In the end, nearly all of them signed. And Davide, on the back of the notebook, drew their faces.

So, for a week, at the gate of the San Frediano school, an unusual scene could be seen: a thirteen-year-old boy with a notebook, another thirteen-year-old boy with a pen and a thirty-five-year-old woman with a thermos labelled "herbal tea", stopping parents one by one. People talked about rents, gyms, pavements. People signed. People drank the tea, which was ribollita. And on 27 February, three days before the deadline, Pietro counted the signatures for the third time, to be sure, and announced the result in the voice of a television presenter: "Two hundred and fourteen. We did it."

The candidacy was submitted to the electoral office on 28 February. Mancini, who could finally write about it, published an article with a headline that made the whole neighbourhood laugh: "People say she is standing. Now it's official." And below, a photograph of Valeria at the market, with the yellow leaflet in one hand and the thermos of tea in the other. Graziella cut it out and put it on the kitchen shelf, next to Pietro's crooked cup. "Now the shelf has politics too," she said. "All that's missing is sport and religion." "Religion is there," said Bellini. "The ribollita."

That evening Valeria stayed in the trattoria until late, after everyone had gone. Graziella was washing the pots. Valeria opened the notebook in which she had written the names and problems of all the people she had met: two hundred and fourteen names and at least three hundred problems. Guido the shoemaker. The fruit seller and the van. Rita and the rent. The broken pavement in front of the school. "I'm scared," she said to Graziella. "Before, when I worked for Milan, it was easy. You looked at the figures, decided, signed. Now every figure has a face."

Graziella turned off the tap, wiped her hands on her apron and sat down opposite her. "My dear," she said, "do you know how ribollita is made? It isn't made in one day. You put everything in the pot in the evening, you let it rest all night, and the next day you boil it again. That's why it's called that. It's only good the next day." She paused. "Politics, in my opinion, is the same. You put together the faces, the problems, the people. You let it rest. And then, with patience, you boil it again." Valeria laughed, for the first time all evening. "I'll write that in the programme," she said. "First line: 'It's done like ribollita.'"

And she really did write it. Valeria Conti's election programme, printed in March by the same print shop in San Frediano, began with a sentence no other candidate would have dared to write: "In the Oltrarno people say politics changes nothing. Perhaps it's true. But people also say ribollita is only good the next day. Let's give ourselves a next day." Below, numbered, were the problems from the notebook, one by one, with the name of the person who had told them. The first was Guido's, the shoemaker from via Toscanella. The last, number three hundred and two, was the fruit seller's: parking the van. And immediately below, handwritten by Graziella in red pen: "Number three hundred and three: my shoes."
